reason: The run renders the same act before Jesus three ways: "pay homage" (Matt 2), "bow down before" (Matt 8:2; 14:33; 28:9, 17; John 9:38) and "worship" (Luke 24:52; Heb 1:6). Matt 28:17 and Luke 24:52 describe the same kind of scene but differ. Acts 7:43 has "bow down to" for idols where Revelation has "worship", and Luke 4:7 has "bow in worship" where Matt 4:9 has "worship". The spelling also varies between "worshiped" and "worshipped".
sense: to prostrate oneself in reverence before someone; the entry governs the whole range, from religious worship of a deity to bowing before a human superior

alternates.when: The gesture is made to a human being, or to Jesus by a petitioner or subordinate during his ministry, and the scene contains no confession of divine status: Matt 8:2; 9:18; 15:25; 18:26; 20:20; Mark 5:6; Rev 3:9. Also acceptable at Mark 15:19.
The recipient is honoured as a king or dignitary, sincerely or in mockery, especially where falling or kneeling is already stated separately: Matt 2:2, 8, 11; Mark 15:19; Acts 10:25.
Only at Heb 11:21, where worship of God is tied to a physical posture over the staff and plain "worship" would read awkwardly.

rationale: The Greek verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. Before God, gods, idols, the beast, or an angel who refuses it, "worship" is exact; it must stay the same word in Rev 19:10 and 22:8-9 so the rebuke "Worship God" answers the act. "Worship" is also kept where Jesus is confessed as God's Son or Lord, is risen, or is the object in a scriptural citation (Matt 14:33; 28:9, 17; Luke 24:52; John 9:38; Heb 1:6), because the context marks the homage as the highest kind. Where a petitioner, slave, or visitor to a king prostrates himself, modern "worship" claims more than the word says, so the physical gesture is rendered instead.
standard_view: The KJV has "worship" almost throughout. Modern versions (NRSV, NIV, ESV, NET) generally keep "worship" for God, idols, the beast, and for Jesus at Matt 14:33; 28:9, 17; Luke 24:52; John 9:38; Heb 1:6. They use "knelt before" or "bowed down" for petitioners and for Matt 18:26 and Mark 5:6. They split on Matt 2, where NRSV has "pay homage" and NIV and ESV have "worship". Scholars disagree on how much divine recognition Matthew intends in the petitioner scenes, and some would use the physical-gesture rendering even at Matt 14:33 and 28:17, as the run did.
